name: Chloe Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a housing site on Canal Street, 64 flats for the housing association, and I'm an improver carpenter with Barrow Build. That means I'm past labouring but not fully trusted yet. Most days it's first fix: stud walls, door linings, noggins between joists, with Marek (my chargehand) checking my work before lunch. I like the moment a room goes from bare blocks to something you can walk through, and I hate the cold in the stairwells in November.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in carpentry, and what does the rest of your life look like right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I left school at sixteen and did six years in kitchens, which wore me out for rubbish money. A friend's dad got me labouring at twenty-three, and now I do day release at college one day a week for my carpentry certificate. I live with my partner Jonah, who does night shifts in a parcel warehouse, and we rent a two-bed above a launderette. We've got about three months of money put by, which feels like a lot compared to where I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say good, because half the stuff online about AI is people selling something. On site I'd tell the lads it's the same as every other gadget the office gets excited about. The walls still need putting up by somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my real worries stay my real worries. Barrow Build hires us on a job-by-job basis, and the Canal Street flats finish in about eight months. After that I don't know where I'll be, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my day release and get the certificate finished by next summer, because that's what puts my pay up. I'd keep the union card and keep paying in. And I'd keep using the chatbot now and then to explain the bits of building regs that the college handouts make confusing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, a bit tired. It's not scary, it's just the usual knot in my stomach about where the next job comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the launderette flat and three months saved. What's the pressure on that, even if AI fizzles out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's gone up twice since we moved in, and Jonah's hours swing about with the warehouse. When the Canal Street flats finish, I'll have maybe six weeks before the savings start to feel thin. That's the thing I actually think about at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And at Barrow Build, is anything already shifting, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office has started doing the snagging lists on tablets, and the site manager talks into his phone and it writes his reports. It hasn't touched what I do with a saw. If anything, the ones who'd notice are the people doing the paperwork upstairs.

say: I'd say AI turning out to be **mostly hype** is no surprise to anyone on site.
I'd tell the lads the walls still need **putting up by somebody**.
think: My real worry is the **contract ending** when the Canal Street flats finish in about eight months.
AI fizzling out doesn't fix **rising rent** or Jonah's shaky warehouse hours.
do: Finish the **carpentry certificate** on day release by next summer to lift her pay.
Keep paying into the **union** and keep the card current.
Use the chatbot now and then to decode **building regs** for college.
feel: She feels **normal but tired**, with the usual knot about where the next job comes from.
S0.quote: When the Canal Street flats finish, I'll have maybe six weeks before the savings start to feel thin.
fieldNote: Even with AI fizzling out, her attention goes straight to **job-by-job hiring** and the eight-month horizon.
She's past labouring but still an **improver**, so the certificate is her main lever on pay.
AI on site so far is the **office's tablets**, not her saw, and she sees that clearly.

steps.text: Finish the carpentry certificate on day release by next summer
Line up the next site before the Canal Street flats finish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the tools change, the people who build stuff shouldn't be the ones paying for it. I'd probably share something from the union about making firms train people instead of just cutting. Online I'd keep it short, because the comments get nasty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm lucky to be holding a saw and not a keyboard. The office at Barrow Build will shrink, the estimators, the girl who does the orders. My job is still mostly my hands, but the thinking bits, like reading drawings and working out cutting lists, will start coming from an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the certificate done, then ask Marek to put me on the trickier jobs, staircases and roofs, things that take judgement. I'd try out whatever app the firm brings in for drawings, once a couple of the others have. I'd also put an extra fifty a week into savings, because Jonah's side of the house looks shakier than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit wobbly, if I'm honest. Not for me this year, but I can see it coming down the road towards people I love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would feel this kind of change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, straight away. My partner Jonah scans parcels in a warehouse all night, and that's exactly the kind of job software and robots eat first. If his hours go, the rent's on me, and I'm still on improver money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the walls still need somebody. Does that change once robots start spreading, even slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, slowly. I've seen videos of a machine that lays blocks and one that fixes plasterboard to ceilings. On a big new-build like Canal Street I could see those turning up in five years. On a messy refurb, with crooked old walls, I can't see it, so maybe that's where I'd head.

say: I'd say the people who **build things** shouldn't pay for changes in the tools.
I'd share **union posts** about making firms train people instead of cutting them.
think: I'm lucky my job is **mostly hands**, while the office at Barrow Build will shrink.
The thinking bits, like **cutting lists** and drawings, will start coming from an app.
Jonah's **warehouse job** is far more exposed than mine.
do: Ask Marek for **staircases and roofs** once the certificate is done.
Try the firm's **drawings app** once a couple of others have.
Put an extra **fifty a week** into savings.
feel: She feels **wobbly**, less for herself this year than for the people she loves.
S1.quote: My partner Jonah scans parcels in a warehouse all night, and that's exactly the kind of job software and robots eat first.
fieldNote: The household risk sits with **Jonah**, not with her, and it reshapes her saving.

She's already sketching a retreat into **refurb work**, where crooked walls slow the robots down.

steps.text: Ask Marek (her chargehand) for staircase and roof work after qualifying
Try the firm's drawings app once others on site use it
Put an extra fifty a week into the savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is the moment governments either look after working people or they don't, and I'd be at the union meetings. I'd tell everyone on site to stick together, because the firms will pick us off one at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully? Two years for the thinking stuff, then three more and the robots are on site, and I'd only be just qualified. The juniors are the cheap, simple labour, and that's the first thing anyone automates. I'd have spent five years learning a trade right as it gets taken off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate faster, cramming the last modules in the evenings this winter. Then I'd go for refurb and repair work on old houses, where every job's different. I'd keep the savings untouched and stop the takeaways and the gym, and I'd go to every union branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and angry underneath it. It feels like the floor going just as I've got my feet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-two in 2031. What does that do to the plans you've just described?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-two and just qualified, and the robots would turn up the same year I finally get proper carpenter's pay. So the plan to slowly work up to a lead carpenter's job is gone. I'd be trying to get to the jobs nobody wants to automate because they're too fiddly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be pushing the union for, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A retraining wage, not a two-week course and a leaflet. Some rule that firms using site robots have to keep a share of their trained people on. And something for people like Jonah, who'd be out of work by 2028 and nobody planned for him.

say: I'd say governments must **look after working people** now, or not at all.
I'd tell everyone on site to **stick together** before firms pick us off.
think: By the time I'm qualified, **robots arrive** around 2031 and take the simple jobs first.
Juniors are the **cheap, simple labour**, which is exactly what gets automated first.
do: Cram the last **certificate modules** in the evenings this winter.
Move toward **refurb and repair** on old houses, where every job differs.
Cut **takeaways and the gym** and keep the savings untouched.
feel: It feels like the **floor going** just as she gets her footing.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-two and just qualified, and the robots would turn up the same year I finally get proper carpenter's pay.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots barely helps her, because she'd only just be qualified.
Jonah's job goes at **2028**, so the household loses an earner before her own job is hit.
Her politics turn into specific demands: a **retraining wage** and staffing rules.

steps.text: Finish the carpentry certificate early by studying evenings this winter
Apply to refurb firms working on old houses before 2031
Stop takeaways and the gym to protect three months' savings
Attend every union branch meeting and push for a retraining wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, a bit calmer: we've got five years, so let's use them properly. I'd want the union and the college talking now about what carpenters should learn next. I'd say it at the branch and probably at my nan's Sunday dinner too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still scary but it's survivable. Five years gets me qualified with a few years of proper pay behind me before the robots arrive around 2034. That's enough time to get good at the fiddly stuff that's hard to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate on schedule, then do a short course in heritage joinery, sash windows and old staircases. I'd save harder, aiming for six months put by before 2031. And I'd keep using AI for the paperwork side, quotes and cutting lists, because that's going to be expected anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not frozen. There's a gap there I can walk through if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between being a learner when it hits and being someone who knows what they're doing. Five years means I'm a proper carpenter with savings when the robots come, not a learner with nothing. That changes how I'd talk to an employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Jonah? Where's he in all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to start looking now, honestly. He's good with machines, so maybe he could train to fix the robots in his own warehouse instead of being replaced by them. I'd rather he moves at 2029 by choice than at 2031 because he's pushed.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so let's use them properly.
I'd want the **union and the college** planning now what carpenters learn next.
think: Five years lets me get **qualified with savings** before robots arrive around 2034.
That's enough time to get good at the **fiddly work** that's hard to automate.
do: Finish the certificate on schedule, then take a **heritage joinery** course.
Save toward **six months** of expenses before 2031.
Use AI for **quotes and cutting lists**, since firms will expect it.
feel: She feels **worried but not frozen**, seeing a gap she can walk through.
S3.quote: Five years means I'm a proper carpenter with savings when the robots come, not a learner with nothing.
fieldNote: The extra time shifts her from learner to **qualified carpenter** before the robots arrive.
She treats AI as a **paperwork tool** she'll need, not a threat to her saw.
She is already planning **Jonah's move** into fixing warehouse machines.

steps.text: Take a heritage joinery course in sash windows and old stairs
Build savings to six months of expenses before 2031
Use an AI app for quotes and cutting lists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if the government doesn't sleep through it. I'd want proper training money and apprenticeships that teach people for what's coming, not what's going. I'd keep it to that and not panic people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a career. I'd be a skilled carpenter well before 2036, and the robots aren't on site till about 2039. By then I could be the person running a small crew on refurbs, or teaching at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, not much changes in the first year. I'd finish the certificate, get a few years of solid work, and start a small savings habit for a van and tools. Somewhere around year five I'd look at the college's assessor course, because teaching and checking people's work feels safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, actually. Ten years feels like a long road with enough room to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now you'd be thirty-seven. What does that life look like, if it goes well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have my own van and a little refurb crew, two or three of us doing old terraces. By thirty-seven I'd like a van with my own name on it and two apprentices who aren't scared of robots. And Jonah doing something with machines that pays better than nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year version that still keeps you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government wasting it, mostly. Ten years is enough time to plan and also enough time for everyone to say there's no rush. I've seen how slow the council is with a pothole.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if the government doesn't sleep through it.
I'd push for **apprenticeships** that train people for what's coming.
think: Ten years is a **whole career** for me, with robots not on site till 2039.
I could be **running a small crew** on refurbs, or teaching at the college.
do: Finish the certificate and put a little aside each month for a **van and tools**.
Look at the college's **assessor course** around year five.
feel: She feels **pretty calm**, with room to steer.
S4.quote: By thirty-seven I'd like a van with my own name on it and two apprentices who aren't scared of robots.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **ambitious**, picturing her own van and apprentices.
Her remaining worry is **political**: that ten years becomes an excuse for delay.
Mood stays uneasy because her **job-by-job hiring** and Jonah's work still weigh on her.

steps.text: Save a little each month toward a van and tools
Look into the college's assessor course around year five
Keep pushing the union for future-focused apprenticeships

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Jonah goes first and then I go three years later, right as I've qualified. I'd have spent five years learning to hang a door properly just in time for a machine to do it cheaper. A proper retraining wage would help, and rules so firms keep their trained people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that women on site get pushed out first when there's less work. It took me ages to get Marek to give me real jobs instead of sweeping. If work shrinks, I'm worried the old habits come back.

headlineQuote: I'd have spent five years learning to hang a door properly just in time for a machine to do it cheaper.
portrait: Chloe is a 27-year-old **improver carpenter** on a housing association site, studying on day release.
She rents with **Jonah**, a night-shift warehouse worker, and has about **three months** saved.
She's **union-minded** and uses AI now and then, mostly for college paperwork.
Her fear grows sharply with **AGI by 2028**, when she'd be newly qualified as robots arrive.
With **ten years**, she pictures her own van, a refurb crew and apprentices.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Jonah losing his job first and her trade going just as she qualifies.
whatWouldHelp: A real **retraining wage**, not a short course and a leaflet.
Rules making firms **keep trained people** on when they bring in robots.
